verses.18:22: Yet again Ahimaaz son of Zadok spoke and said to Joab, "Come what may, please let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why would you run, my son, when there is no reward for news coming to you?"
verses.18:23: "Come what may, I will run." And he said to him, "Run!" So Ahimaaz ran along the way of the plain and went past the Cushite.
verses.18:24: Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went to the roof of the gate by the wall. He lifted his eyes and looked, and there was a man running alone.
verses.18:25: The watchman called out and reported to the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, news is in his mouth." And he kept coming nearer and nearer.
verses.18:26: Then the watchman saw another man running; and the watchman called out to the gatekeeper and said, "Look, a man is running alone!" And the king said, "This one also is bringing news."
verses.18:27: The watchman said, "I see that the running of the first one is like the running of Ahimaaz son of Zadok." And the king said, "This one is a good man, and he is coming with good news."
verses.18:28: Then Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down to the king with his face to the ground and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who lifted up their hand against my lord the king."
verses.18:29: The king said, "Is all well with the young man Absalom?" And Ahimaaz said, "I saw the great commotion when Joab sent the king's servant and your servant, yet I did not know what it was."
verses.18:30: Then the king said, "Turn aside; take your stand here." So he turned aside and stood.
verses.18:31: And now the Cushite arrived, and the Cushite said, "May my lord the king receive news, for the LORD has vindicated you today from the hand of all who rose up against you."
verses.18:32: The king said to the Cushite, "Is all well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite said, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rose up against you for harm be like the young man."
verses.19:1: The king was shaken, and he went up to the upper chamber of the gate and wept. As he walked, he said, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I myself had died in your place! Absalom, my son, my son!"
verses.19:2: It was reported to Joab, "Look, the king is weeping and mourning over Absalom."
verses.19:3: So the victory on that day became mourning for all the people, because on that day the people heard it said, "The king is grieved over his son."
verses.19:4: And the people slipped quietly into the city on that day, just as humiliated people slip quietly away when they flee in battle.
verses.19:5: Meanwhile, the king had covered his face, and the king cried out with a loud voice, "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"
verses.19:6: Then Joab came to the king in the house and said, "Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants who rescued your life today, and the lives of your sons and your daughters, and the lives of your wives, and the lives of your concubines,
verses.19:7: by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you. For you have declared today that commanders and servants mean nothing to you; for I know today that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then it would be right in your eyes.
verses.19:8: So now get up, go out, and speak to the heart of your servants. For I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, surely not one man will stay the night with you tonight; and this will be worse for you than all the calamity that has come upon you from your youth until now."
verses.19:9: So the king got up and sat in the gate. And they informed all the people, "Look, the king is sitting in the gate." Then all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled, each man to his tents.
verses.19:10: And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies, and he rescued us from the hand of the Philistines; yet now he has fled from the land away from Absalom.
verses.19:11: And Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. So now, why are you staying silent about bringing the king back?"
verses.19:12: Then King David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, "Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, since the word of all Israel has come to the king, to his house?
verses.19:13: You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. So why should you be the last to bring the king back?'
verses.19:14: And to Amasa say, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? May God do so to me, and may He add to it, if you are not commander of the army before me continually in place of Joab!'"
verses.19:15: And he inclined the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so they sent word to the king, "Return, you and all your servants."
verses.19:16: Then the king returned and came as far as the Jordan. And Judah came to Gilgal to go to meet the king, to bring the king across the Jordan.
verses.19:17: And Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite who was from Bahurim, hurried and went down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
verses.19:18: With him were a thousand men from Benjamin, along with Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they rushed across the Jordan before the king.
verses.19:19: And the ferryboat crossed to bring the king's household over and to do what was good in his eyes. And Shimei son of Gera fell down before the king as he was crossing the Jordan.
verses.19:20: And he said to the king, "May my lord not count iniquity against me, and do not remember how your servant acted perversely on the day my lord the king went out from Jerusalem, so that the king would take it to heart.
verses.19:21: For your servant knows that I have sinned; so look, I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king."
verses.19:22: Then Abishai son of Zeruiah answered and said, "Should Shimei not be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"
verses.19:23: But David said, "What is there between me and you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should become an adversary to me today? Should any man be put to death in Israel today? For do I not know that today I am king over Israel?"
verses.19:24: And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king swore to him.
verses.19:25: Now Mephibosheth son of Saul went down to meet the king. He had neither tended his feet nor trimmed his mustache, nor had he washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in peace.
verses.19:26: And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
verses.19:27: He answered, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, 'I will saddle the donkey for myself and ride on it and go with the king,' because your servant is lame.
verses.19:28: Moreover, he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God; therefore do what is good in your eyes.
verses.19:29: For all my father's house were nothing but men doomed to death before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further rightful claim do I have, then, to cry out any longer to the king?"
verses.19:30: Then the king said to him, "Why do you speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."
verses.19:31: And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him even take it all, now that my lord the king has come back in peace to his house."
verses.19:32: Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he crossed the Jordan with the king to escort him across the Jordan.
verses.19:33: Now Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age; and he had provided for the king during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a very great man.
verses.19:34: And the king said to Barzillai, "You, cross over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem."
verses.19:35: But Barzillai said to the king, "How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
verses.19:36: I am eighty years old today. Can I distinguish between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat and what I drink? Can I still hear the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be a further burden to my lord the king?
verses.19:37: Your servant will go just a short way across the Jordan with the king; so why should the king repay me with this reward?
verses.19:38: Please let your servant return, so that I may die in my own city, beside the grave of my father and my mother. Yet here is your servant Chimham; let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your eyes."
verses.19:39: And the king said, "Chimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your eyes; and whatever you choose to ask of me, I will do for you."
verses.19:40: Then all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king also crossed over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his place.
verses.19:41: Then the king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. And all the people of Judah had brought the king across, along with half the people of Israel.
verses.19:42: Now all the men of Israel were coming to the king, and they said to the king, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all David's men with him?"
verses.19:43: Then all the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is a close relative to us. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense, or has any gift been given to us?"
verses.19:44: Then the men of Israel answered the men of Judah and said, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David as well we have more than you. Why then did you treat us lightly? Was it not our word first to bring back our king?" Yet the speech of the men of Judah was harsher than the speech of the men of Israel.
verses.20:1: Now a worthless man happened to be there whose name was Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blew the ram's horn and said, "We have no share in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Each man to his tents, Israel!"
verses.20:2: So all the men of Israel withdrew from following David to go after Sheba son of Bichri, but the men of Judah clung to their king from the Jordan all the way to Jerusalem.
verses.20:3: When David came to his house in Jerusalem, the king took the ten women, the concubines whom he had left to keep the house, and placed them in a guarded house and provided for them, but he did not go in to them. So they remained shut up until the day of their death, in living widowhood.
verses.20:4: Then the king said to Amasa, "Summon the men of Judah to me within three days, and you yourself be present here."
verses.20:5: So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the appointed time that he had set for him.
verses.20:6: Then David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue after him, so that he does not find fortified cities for himself and escape from our sight."
verses.20:7: So Joab's men went out after him, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men; they went out from Jerusalem to pursue after Sheba son of Bichri.
verses.20:8: When they were by the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was dressed in his tunic that he wore, and over it was a sword belt with a sword fastened at his waist in its sheath; and as he went forward, it fell out.
verses.20:9: And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab's right hand took hold of Amasa's beard to kiss him.
verses.20:10: Now Amasa was not on guard against the sword that was in Joab's hand; so he struck him with it in the belly and spilled out his entrails onto the ground, and he did not strike him a second time, and he died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued after Sheba son of Bichri.
verses.20:11: And one of Joab's young men stood beside him and said, "Whoever favors Joab and whoever is for David, after Joab!"
verses.20:12: Now Amasa was wallowing in blood in the middle of the highway. And when the man saw that all the people stood still, he moved Amasa off the highway into the field and threw a garment over him, when he saw that everyone who came up to him stood still.
verses.20:13: Once he had been removed from the highway, every man passed on after Joab to pursue after Sheba son of Bichri.
verses.20:14: Now he passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel and Beth-maacah, and all the Berites; and they assembled and came after him as well.
verses.20:15: Then they came and besieged him in Abel Beth-maacah, and they heaped up a siege mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart. And all the people who were with Joab were battering to bring the wall down.
verses.20:16: Then a wise woman called out from the city, "Listen, listen! Please say to Joab, 'Come near here, so that I may speak to you.'"
verses.20:17: So he came near to her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" And he answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your maidservant." And he said, "I am listening."
verses.20:18: Then she spoke, saying, "In former times they used to say, 'Let them surely inquire at Abel,' and thus they settled matters.
verses.20:19: I am one of the peaceable and faithful of Israel. You are seeking to put to death a city and a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the LORD?"
verses.20:20: Joab answered and said, "Far be it, far be it from me that I should swallow up or destroy!
verses.20:21: That is not the case. Rather, a man from the hill country of Ephraim, whose name is Sheba son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against the king, against David. Hand him over alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Look, his head will be thrown to you over the wall."
verses.20:22: Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. So he blew the ram's horn, and they dispersed from the city, each man to his tents. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verses.20:23: Now Joab was over all the army of Israel, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites.
verses.20:24: Adoram was over the forced labor, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
verses.20:25: Sheva was scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
verses.20:26: And Ira the Jairite was also a priest to David.
verses.21:1: Now a famine came in the days of David for three years, year after year, and David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, "It is on account of Saul and on account of the house of bloodguilt, because he put the Gibeonites to death."
verses.21:2: Then the king summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not from the sons of Israel, but rather from the remnant of the Amorites; and the sons of Israel had sworn to them, yet Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the sons of Israel and Judah.
verses.21:3: David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you, and with what shall I make atonement, so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?"
verses.21:4: The Gibeonites said to him, "We have no claim of silver or gold with Saul or with his house, nor is it ours to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
verses.21:5: And they said to the king, "As for the man who consumed us and who schemed against us that we would be destroyed from remaining within all the territory of Israel,
verses.21:6: let seven men from his sons be given to us, and we will impale them for the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen one of the LORD." And the king said, "I myself will give them."
verses.21:7: However, the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, on account of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.
verses.21:8: So the king took the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Michal daughter of Saul, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.
verses.21:9: He gave them into the hand of the Gibeonites, and they impaled them on the mountain before the LORD, and all seven of them fell together. They were put to death during the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.
verses.21:10: Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured down on them from the sky; and she did not allow the birds of the sky to rest on them by day, nor the wild animals of the field by night.
verses.21:11: It was told to David what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done.
verses.21:12: So David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son from the citizens of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day the Philistines struck Saul down on Gilboa.
verses.21:13: He brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son, and they gathered the bones of those who had been impaled.
verses.21:14: They buried the bones of Saul and of Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin at Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father, and they did everything that the king commanded. And God heeded the plea for the land after that.
verses.21:15: Now the Philistines had war again with Israel, and David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought with the Philistines; and David became exhausted.
verses.21:16: And Ishbi-benob, who was among the descendants of Rapha, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze and who was strapped with a new sword, intended to strike down David.
verses.21:17: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, and he struck down the Philistine and put him to death. Then the men of David swore to him, saying, "You must not go out with us to war anymore, so that you will not quench the lamp of Israel."
verses.21:18: Now after this, there was war again at Gob with the Philistines; then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was among the descendants of Rapha.
verses.21:19: And there was war again at Gob with the Philistines, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite; and the shaft of his spear was like a weavers' beam.
verses.21:20: There was war again at Gath, and there was a man of tall stature; the fingers on each of his hands and the toes on each of his feet were six, twenty-four in number, and he too was born to Rapha.
verses.21:21: He taunted Israel, and Jonathan son of Shimeah, the brother of David, struck him down.
verses.21:22: These four were born to Rapha in Gath, and they fell at the hand of David and at the hand of his servants.
verses.22:1: David spoke the words of this song to the LORD on the day the LORD rescued him from the grasp of all his enemies and from the grasp of Saul.
verses.22:2: He said, "The LORD is my crag and my stronghold and my own deliverer;
verses.22:3: The God of my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn of my salvation, my secure height and my place of escape, my savior—You save me from violence.
verses.22:4: I call to the LORD, the One to be praised, and from my enemies I am saved.
verses.22:5: For the breakers of death enclosed me; the torrents of ruin terrified me.
verses.22:6: The ropes of Sheol encircled me; the traps of death confronted me.
verses.22:7: In my distress I called to the LORD, and to my God I called; He heard my voice from His temple, and my cry for help was in His ears.
verses.22:8: Then the earth heaved and quaked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and heaved, because He burned with anger.
verses.22:9: Smoke rose from His nostrils, and fire from His mouth devoured; coals blazed from Him.
verses.22:10: He bent the heavens and descended, and dense darkness was beneath His feet.
verses.22:11: He rode a cherub and flew, and He was seen upon the wings of the wind.
verses.22:12: He set darkness around Himself as pavilions—a gathering of waters, thick clouds of the skies.
verses.22:13: From the radiance before Him, coals of fire blazed.
verses.22:14: The LORD thundered from the heavens, and the Most High gave forth His voice.
verses.22:15: He sent forth arrows and scattered them, lightning, and threw them into panic.
verses.22:16: And the channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were uncovered at the LORD's rebuke, from the blast of the wind of His nostrils.
verses.22:17: He reached out from the heights and took hold of me; He pulled me out of great waters.
verses.22:18: He rescued me from my mighty enemy, from those who hated me, for they were stronger than I.
verses.22:19: They confronted me on the day of my disaster, but the LORD became a support to me.
verses.22:20: He brought me out into a spacious place; He freed me, because He took pleasure in me.
verses.22:21: The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the purity of my hands He repaid me.
verses.22:22: For I kept the ways of the LORD and did not turn wickedly from my God.
verses.22:23: For all His judgments were before me; as for His statutes, I did not turn aside from them.
verses.22:24: And I was blameless toward Him, and I guarded myself from my iniquity.
verses.22:25: So the LORD repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my purity before His eyes.
verses.22:26: With the loyal You prove Yourself loyal; with the blameless mighty man You prove Yourself blameless.
verses.22:27: With the pure You prove Yourself pure, and with the crooked You prove Yourself shrewd.
verses.22:28: And You save an afflicted people, while Your eyes are upon the lofty—You bring them low.
verses.22:29: For You are my lamp, LORD, and the LORD illuminates my darkness.
verses.22:30: For with You I run against a raiding band; with my God I leap over a wall.
verses.22:31: God—His way is blameless; the word of the LORD is refined; He is a shield for all who take refuge in Him.
verses.22:32: For who is God apart from the LORD? And who is a rock apart from our God?
verses.22:33: God is my fortress of strength, and He clears my way to be blameless.
verses.22:34: He makes my feet like those of deer, and upon my high places He makes me stand.
verses.22:35: He teaches my hands for battle, so that my arms bend a bronze bow.
verses.22:36: You gave me the shield of Your salvation, and Your answering made me great.
verses.22:37: You widened my stride beneath me, and my ankles did not slip.
verses.22:38: I pursued my enemies and annihilated them, and I did not turn back until they were finished off.
verses.22:39: I finished them off and smashed them, and they could not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
verses.22:40: You girded me with strength for battle; You made those who rose against me kneel beneath me.
verses.22:41: And You caused my enemies to show me their backs; as for those who hated me, I wiped them out.
verses.22:42: They looked around, yet there was no one to save—to the LORD, yet He did not answer them.
verses.22:43: I ground them fine like the dust of the earth; like the mud of the streets I pounded them, I trampled them.
verses.22:44: You delivered me from the disputes of my people; You preserved me to be head of nations; a people I had not known serves me.
verses.22:45: Foreigners come cringing to me; as soon as their ears hear, they obey me.
verses.22:46: Foreigners wither away and come limping out of their fortresses.
verses.22:47: The LORD lives, and may my rock be blessed; may the God of the rock of my salvation be exalted—
verses.22:48: the God who grants vengeance to me and brings peoples down beneath me,
verses.22:49: and who brings me out from my enemies. You lift me high above those who rise against me; from the man of violence You rescue me.
verses.22:50: Therefore I will thank You, LORD, among the nations, and to Your name I will sing praise.
verses.22:51: He is the tower of His king's salvation, and He shows loyal love to His anointed, to David and to his offspring forever."
verses.23:1: These are the final words of David: The declaration of David son of Jesse, and the declaration of the man who was raised up on high, the anointed one of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of the songs of Israel.
verses.23:2: The Spirit of the LORD has spoken through me, and His word is on my tongue.
verses.23:3: The God of Israel has said; to me the Rock of Israel spoke, "One who rules over humanity righteously, one who rules in the fear of God,
verses.23:4: is like the light of morning as the sun rises, a morning with no clouds, through radiance after rain bringing tender grass out of the earth."
verses.23:5: For is not my house like this with God? For He has established an everlasting covenant for me, arranged in everything and kept secure; for all my deliverance and every desire, will He not cause them to sprout?
verses.23:6: But the worthless, all of them, are like thorns cast aside, for no one takes them by hand;
verses.23:7: and the man who touches them must equip himself with iron and a spear shaft, and with fire they will be utterly burned on the spot.
verses.23:8: These are the names of the mighty men who belonged to David: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite, chief of the captains; he was Adino the Eznite, over eight hundred killed on a single occasion.
verses.23:9: And after him was Eleazar son of Dodo, son of an Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David when they defied the Philistines who had gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew.
verses.23:10: He rose up and struck down the Philistines until his hand grew tired and his hand clung to the sword, and the LORD accomplished a great deliverance on that day; and the people returned after him only to plunder.
verses.23:11: And after him was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered into a troop where a plot of the field was full of lentils, and the people fled from the Philistines.
verses.23:12: But he stood his ground in the middle of the plot, defended it, and struck down the Philistines; and the LORD accomplished a great deliverance.
verses.23:13: Then three of the thirty chief men went down and came at harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, while a troop of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.
verses.23:14: Now David was in the stronghold at that time, and a garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem.
verses.23:15: David longed deeply and said, "Who will give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is at the gate?"
verses.23:16: Then the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem that was at the gate, and carried and brought it to David. Yet he was unwilling to drink it, and poured it out as a drink offering to the LORD.
verses.23:17: And he said, "Far be it from me, LORD, to do this! Is this the blood of the men who went at the cost of their lives?" So he was unwilling to drink it. These things the three mighty men did.
verses.23:18: Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three. He brandished his spear against three hundred and killed them, and he had a name among the three.
verses.23:19: Was he not the most honored of the three? So he became their commander, yet he did not attain to the three.
verses.23:20: And Benaiah son of Jehoiada, son of a man of valor, great in deeds, from Kabzeel, struck down the two Ariels of Moab; he also went down and struck down a lion in the middle of a pit on a snowy day.
verses.23:21: He also struck down an Egyptian, a man of imposing appearance. In the Egyptian's hand was a spear, yet he went down to him with a club, snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand, and killed him with his own spear.
verses.23:22: These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did, and he had a name among the three mighty men.
verses.23:23: He was more honored than the thirty, yet he did not attain to the three; and David appointed him over his bodyguard.
verses.23:24: Asahel the brother of Joab was among the thirty; Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
verses.23:25: Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,
verses.23:26: Helez the Paltite, Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite,
verses.23:27: Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
verses.23:28: Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,
verses.23:29: Heleb son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the sons of Benjamin,
verses.23:30: Benaiah a Pirathonite, Hiddai from the brooks of Gaash,
verses.23:31: Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,
verses.23:32: Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,
verses.23:33: Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam son of Sharar the Ararite,
verses.23:34: Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, son of the Maacathite, Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
verses.23:35: Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,
verses.23:36: Igal son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
verses.23:37: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah,
verses.23:38: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verses.23:39: Uriah the Hittite; thirty-seven in all.
verses.24:1: Once again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He incited David against them, saying, "Go, count Israel and Judah."
verses.24:2: Then the king said to Joab, the army commander who was with him, "Please travel throughout all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and enroll the people, so that I may know the count of the people."
verses.24:3: Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times over as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king look on! Yet why does my lord the king take pleasure in this matter?"
verses.24:4: Yet the word of the king prevailed against Joab and against the army commanders. So Joab and the army commanders went out from before the king to enroll the people, Israel.
verses.24:5: They crossed the Jordan and made camp at Aroer, on the south side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and toward Jazer.
verses.24:6: Next they went into Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and they went on to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon.
verses.24:7: They came to the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites, and they went out to the Negev of Judah, at Beersheba.
verses.24:8: So they traveled throughout the entire land, and at the end of nine months and twenty days they came to Jerusalem.
verses.24:9: Joab gave the king the count of the enrollment of the people: Israel was eight hundred thousand men of valor who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men.
verses.24:10: Then David's heart struck him after he had counted the people. David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. And now, LORD, please put away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have behaved very foolishly."
verses.24:11: When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David's seer, saying,
verses.24:12: "Go and speak to David, 'This is what the LORD says: Three things I hold out before you; choose one of them for yourself, and I will do it to you.'"
verses.24:13: Then Gad came to David and informed him, and he said to him, "Will seven years of famine come upon you in your land? Or will you flee for three months before your adversaries as they pursue you? Or will there be three days of pestilence in your land? Now know and see what word I should take back to the One who sent me."
verses.24:14: And David said to Gad, "I am in severe distress. Please let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are abundant; yet into the hand of man may I not fall."
verses.24:15: So the LORD brought pestilence on Israel from the morning until the appointed time, and among the people, from Dan to Beersheba, seventy thousand men died.
verses.24:16: When the angel reached out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented concerning the disaster and said to the angel who was bringing destruction among the people, "Enough! Now let your hand drop." Now the angel of the LORD was beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
verses.24:17: Then David spoke to the LORD as he saw the angel who was striking among the people, and he said, "Look, I am the one who has sinned, and I am the one who has done wickedly; yet these sheep, what have they done? Let Your hand please be against me and against the house of my father."
verses.24:18: On that day Gad came to David and said to him, "Go up, set up an altar to the LORD at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."
verses.24:19: So David went up in accordance with Gad's word, as the LORD had commanded.
verses.24:20: Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming over toward him, so Araunah went out and bowed low before the king with his face to the ground.
verses.24:21: Araunah asked, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David replied, "To purchase the threshing floor from you to build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague may be restrained from the people."
verses.24:22: Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up whatever is good in his eyes. See, the oxen are for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the equipment of the oxen are for the wood."
verses.24:23: All of this Araunah the king gave to the king. And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you."
verses.24:24: Yet the king replied to Araunah, "No, for I will certainly purchase it from you for a price, and I will not offer up to the LORD my God burnt offerings at no cost." So David purchased the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
verses.24:25: There David built an altar to the LORD and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD heeded the plea for the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.

notes.1:8: Ketiv reads "and he said," whereas Qere reads "and I said" (translated here, matching the Amalekite's reply).
notes.1:9: The rare Hebrew noun hashavats (a hapax legomenon, from a root meaning to interweave or bind tightly) denotes a seizure, cramp, or death agony. The following clause literally reads "for all-still my life is in me," expressing that his life force had not yet left him.
notes.1:16: Ketiv reads plural "your bloods" (an idiom for bloodguilt), whereas Qere reads singular "your blood" (translated here).
notes.1:18: Hebrew qashet ("bow") is traditionally taken as the title of David's lament (cf. Jonathan's bow in v. 22), though some understand it literally as instruction in archery. The Book of Jashar (lit. "the Book of the Upright") was an ancient collection of Israelite songs (cf. Josh 10:13).
notes.1:21: Hebrew "fields of offerings" (sede terumot) translates the Masoretic Text directly and refers to fertile fields yielding agricultural offerings. The Niphal verb nig'al means "was polluted" or "was defiled."
notes.2:9: The Masoretic Text reads "the Ashurites" (ha'ashuri), possibly referring to the territory of Asher or a northern district; the prepositions "to" (el) and "over" (al) alternate interchangeably in this list.
notes.2:14: The Piel verb yesahaqu literally means "play" or "make sport," used here as a grim military euphemism for a representative contest of combat.
notes.2:16: Helkath-hazzurim is traditionally understood as "Field of Sword-edges" (or "Field of Flint-knives" or "Field of Rocks"), from Hebrew helqah ("plot, field") and tsurim ("flints, sharp edges, rocks").
notes.2:27: Joab's oath is syntactically ambiguous: Hebrew mehabboqer (lit. "from the morning") may refer either to the morning just past (implying the people would have withdrawn immediately had Abner not issued his challenge in v. 14) or to the following morning (implying the pursuit would have continued until dawn had Abner not called for a halt in v. 26).
notes.2:29: Hebrew habbitron ("the Bithron," from a root meaning "cut" or "divide") likely designates a ravine or district east of the Jordan, though some interpreters take it temporally as "the half-day" or "forenoon."
notes.3:2: Ketiv reads wyldw, lacking the second waw of the Niphal (either a defective spelling or a Qal/passive form); the translation follows the Qere, Niphal wayyiqtol "were born."
notes.3:7: MT omits an explicit subject for "he said"; the speaker is identified as Ish-bosheth in verse 8.
notes.3:18: MT reads hoshia (a Hiphil infinitive construct or 3ms perfect form of yasha) alongside the first-person suffixes "My servant" and "My people"; rendered as a first-person finite promise ("I will deliver") following the surrounding first-person divine speech.
notes.3:25: Ketiv reads the standard noun form mevo'ekha; Qere reads mova'ekha, assimilating its pattern to the paired noun motsa'akha ("your going out"). Both mean "your coming in."
notes.3:29: Hebrew pelekh means "spindle" (cf. Proverbs 31:19), implying a man unfit for warfare; some interpreters understand it here as a "crutch" or "staff."
notes.4:2: MT reads "the son of Saul" without the expected possessive preposition lamed ("to"), rendered here as "belonged to the son of Saul."
notes.4:6: MT reads hennah ("in there") with the participial phrase loqeche chittim ("fetching wheat"), summarizing the assassination before expanding it in verse 7, without the doorkeeper episode found in the Septuagint.
notes.4:10: Hebrew besorah ("good news") is used here in the rare sense of "reward for good news," with irony: execution at Ziklag was the only reward David gave the self-styled bearer of good news (mevasser).
notes.5:2: Ketiv divides the letters as "hyyth mwsy'" ("you were one bringing out"), placing the final he on the verb; Qere reads "hayita hammotsi'" ("you were the one bringing out"), placing the definite article on the Hiphil participle to match the following articular participle "wehammevi'" ("and the one bringing in").
notes.5:6: The form "hesirekha" is a Hiphil perfect 3ms with a 2ms object suffix ("will turn you back"), taking "the blind and the lame" as its subject; some alternatively construe it as an infinitive ("unless you remove the blind and the lame").
notes.5:8: The Hebrew clause is elliptical and contains the rare noun "tsinnor" ("water shaft," also in Ps 42:8 MT). For "who are hated," Ketiv reads Qal perfect 3cp "san'u" ("who hate David's soul"), whereas Qere reads Qal passive participle construct "senu'e" ("hated by David's soul").
notes.5:24: Ketiv reads "beshom'akha" ("when you hear"), while Qere reads "keshom'akha" ("as soon as you hear"). The precise tree denoted by "bekha'im" ("balsam trees") is uncertain, and the Qal imperfect "teherats" conveys acting sharply or decisively.
notes.6:2: The Masoretic Text reads "mibba'ale yehudah" ("from Baale-judah") despite the following "to bring up from there," and repeats the noun "shem" ("the name, the name of the LORD of hosts").
notes.6:5: The Masoretic Text literally reads "bekhol 'atse veroshim" ("with all cypress woods"), understood here as instruments made of cypress wood; the parallel in 1 Chr 13:8 reads "with all might and with songs."
notes.6:7: The noun "hashshal" ("the irreverence") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and is generally connected to a root attested in Aramaic meaning error, carelessness, or irreverent fault.
notes.6:19: The rare noun "'eshpar" (occurring only here and 1 Chr 16:3) is of uncertain meaning; modern scholarship divides between "date cake" (parallel to "'ashishah," "raisin cake") and "portion of meat."
notes.6:22: The Masoretic Text reads "be'enay" ("in my own eyes"), whereas the Septuagint reads "in your eyes."
notes.7:7: MT reads "tribes of Israel" (shivtei Yisrael), reflecting the Masoretic consonantal text rather than "judges of Israel" (shofetei) in the parallel at 1 Chr 17:6.
notes.7:16: MT reads "before you" (lefanekha, 2ms), referring to David, whereas the Septuagint and Syriac read "before Me."
notes.7:19: The clause "And this is the instruction of mankind" (torat ha-adam) is syntactically difficult; it is variously understood as a charter for humanity or as an unmarked rhetorical question, "And is this the custom of mankind?"
notes.7:23: MT exhibits abrupt shifts in person and dense syntax: a plural verb with Elohim ("God went"), a 2mp pronoun ("for you"), "for Your land," and "nations and their gods" (lit., "its gods," with singular suffix), without the verb "driving out" found in 1 Chr 17:21.
notes.7:27: Two Hebrew idioms are rendered literally: "uncovered the ear" (galah ozen, meaning to reveal) and "found his heart" (matsa et-libbo, meaning to summon courage).
notes.8:1: "Metheg-ammah" literally means "the bridle of the cubit" or "bridle of the mother-city," either a place name or an idiom for control of the Philistine chief city (cf. 1 Chr 18:1).
notes.8:3: "Euphrates" (Perat) is a Masoretic qere wela ketiv, read though unwritten in the consonantal text ("at the river"); "restore his control" is literally "bring back his hand."
notes.8:13: MT reads "Aram" here (as also in v. 12), whereas the Valley of Salt and v. 14 point geographically toward Edom (as read by the Septuagint, Syriac, and 1 Chr 18:12); the translation follows MT.
notes.8:18: MT reads "and Benaiah son of Jehoiada and the Cherethites and the Pelethites" without the preposition "over" (cf. 20:23), here rendered with "over" understood from v. 16 and the paired conjunctions as "both ... and." MT also calls David's sons "priests" (kohanim), likely denoting priestly or high royal officials (cf. 1 Chr 18:17).
notes.9:7: Hebrew "father" (av) here denotes a grandfather or forefather (Saul, father of Jonathan), just as "son" (ben) in vv. 9-10 refers to Saul's grandson Mephibosheth.
notes.9:11: MT reads "at my table" (shulchani), leaving the second clause either within Ziba's reply or as an unintroduced remark of David; the Septuagint and Syriac read "at David's table" (cf. v. 13).
notes.10:6: The Niphal verb nib'ashu literally means "they had become a stench," an idiom for becoming thoroughly odious and provoking hostility.
notes.10:7: The Masoretic Text places two definite nouns in apposition, literally "all the army, the mighty warriors" (contrast the construct phrase in 1 Chronicles 19:8).
notes.10:9: The ketiv reads "in Israel" (b-yisra'el), whereas the qere reads "Israel" (yisra'el), yielding the construct phrase "the chosen men of Israel."
notes.10:18: Hebrew literally reads "seven hundred chariotry" (rekhev), a collective noun used metonymically with the verb "killed" to designate chariot fighters or crews.
notes.11:1: The Masoretic Text spells this word with a silent aleph while vocalizing it as hammelakhim ("the kings"), rather than hammal'akhim ("the messengers").
notes.11:4: The circumstantial clause uses the Hithpael participle mitqaddeshet ("purifying herself") to indicate Bathsheba's ritual purification from menstrual uncleanness, explaining both her bathing and the timing of her conception.
notes.11:21: The Masoretic Text reads "Jerubbesheth," substituting bosheth ("shame") for Baal in the name Jerubbaal (cf. Judges 9:53).
notes.11:24: Both the verb "shot" (wayyoru) and the participle "archers" (hammorim) are Hiphil forms of yarah ("shoot") written with a quiescent orthographic aleph.
notes.11:25: The particle 'et introduces the subject "this thing" with the intransitive jussive verb yera' ("be evil"), creating a pointed lexical contrast with 11:27; the final Piel imperative "encourage him" shifts back from Joab to the messenger.
notes.12:9: Qere reads "in My eyes," matching the LORD's first-person speech in verses 7-12, whereas Ketiv reads "in His eyes."
notes.12:14: The Hebrew reads "you have caused the enemies of the LORD to show utter contempt" (taking the Piel infinitive absolute plus finite verb of na'ats causatively); the phrase "the enemies of the LORD" is widely viewed as a scribal euphemism to avoid speaking directly of scorning the LORD.
notes.12:24: Qere reads "and she called" (Bathsheba), whereas Ketiv reads "and he called" (David).
notes.12:30: The Masoretic vocalization reads "their king" (malkam); the same consonants can also be vocalized as Milcom (or Malcam), the national deity of the Ammonites.
notes.12:31: Qere reads "the brickkiln" (or "brick-mold"), whereas Ketiv reads a form of uncertain sense ("bmlkn"). The idioms "set them to" and "made them pass through" are understood by some as forced labor and by others as severe punishment.
notes.13:16: The Masoretic syntax of Tamar's protest is compressed, opening with "No!" followed by an elliptical causal expression ("on account of / because") and a comparative clause ("this evil ... greater than the other ... in sending me away").
notes.13:20: The Hebrew spells the name "Aminon" here rather than "Amnon," widely understood as a scornful diminutive spoken by Absalom.
notes.13:33: Qere omits the written particle "im" (Ketiv "ki im", "rather / but only"), reading simply "ki" ("for").
notes.13:37: Qere reads "Ammihud," whereas Ketiv reads "Ammihur." The unstated subject of "mourned" in the second clause is David.
notes.13:39: The verb translated "longed" is pointed as a feminine singular Piel form ("vattekhal") with the masculine subject "King David," commonly understood with an implied feminine subject such as "his soul" or "his spirit" (in the sense of Qal kalah, "pine/long for"), though some interpret the Piel as "ceased" (going out against Absalom).
notes.14:4: The Masoretic Text reads "spoke" (Qal of amar) at the start of the verse before the prostration and the second "said"; translated faithfully as written without emending to "came."
notes.14:14: Literally "God does not lift/take away a life," followed by the Qal intransitive imperfect and Niphal participle of nadach ("so that a banished one will not remain banished").
notes.14:19: The rare form ish here is a variant spelling of the existential particle yesh ("there is"), paired with the oath negative im to mean "there is no turning to the right or to the left."
notes.14:22: Qere reads "your servant," matching "your servant knows" earlier in the verse, whereas Ketiv reads "his servant."
notes.14:30: Qere reads the Hiphil plural imperative with feminine suffix ("set it on fire," matching plural "go"), whereas Ketiv writes an irregular spelling with waw.
notes.15:7: The Masoretic Text reads "forty years," translated literally here without emendation.
notes.15:20: Qere reads the Hiphil imperfect "make you wander" (Ketiv writes a form with waw); the closing blessing follows the concise Masoretic Text without expansion.
notes.15:21: The particle im after ki is written in the consonantal text but omitted in the Qere reading (Ketiv velo Qere); both forms introduce an emphatic oath affirmation.
notes.15:27: The Masoretic Text reads haroeh attah, literally "Are you a seer?" (or "Do you see?"), translated faithfully as written.
notes.15:28: Qere reads "in the plains of the wilderness" (from aravah), whereas Ketiv reads "at the fords of the wilderness" (from avarah).
notes.15:31: The Masoretic Text reads the active Hiphil verb "told" (higgid) with "David" fronted without a preposition, understood impersonally as "someone told David."
notes.16:2: The Qere reads 'and the bread' (we-ha-lechem), whereas the Ketiv contains an apparent scribal dittography of the prefix lamed (w-l-h-l-ch-m).
notes.16:10: The Qere reads 'So let him curse, because' (koh ... ki), whereas the Ketiv reads 'If he curses, and because/if' (ki ... we-ki).
notes.16:12: Following the Qere, 'upon my eye' (be-eini, traditionally understood as David's weeping eye or tears); the Ketiv (b-'-w-n-y) can be read 'upon my affliction' or 'upon the wrong done to me.'
notes.16:18: The Qere reads 'his' (lo), while the Ketiv writes the homophonous spelling l-a ('not').
notes.16:23: The word 'someone' (Hebrew ish, 'a man') is a Masoretic Qere without Ketiv, read aloud in the traditional text though absent from the written consonants.
notes.17:3: The Masoretic Hebrew is terse: literally 'like the return of all [is] the man whom you seek,' meaning that removing David alone ensures the peaceful return of the whole nation.
notes.17:12: The Qere corrects the feminine Ketiv numeral ('one,' b-a-ch-t) to the masculine (be-achad) to agree grammatically with the masculine noun 'places' (meqomot).
notes.17:20: 'Stream' translates the Hebrew hapax legomenon mikhal (literally 'mikhal of water'), traditionally understood as a small stream or water channel.
notes.17:25: The Masoretic Text reads 'Ithra the Israelite' (compare 1 Chronicles 2:17, 'Jether the Ishmaelite').
notes.17:28: The Masoretic Text repeats qali ('roasted/parched produce') twice, first after the cereal grains and again after the beans and lentils, rendered here as 'roasted grain' and 'roasted seeds.'
notes.18:3: Qere reads the Qal infinitive construct "to help" for Ketiv's Hiphil form. The MT also reads the adverb "now" ("for now there are ten thousand like us"), whereas several ancient versions and some Hebrew manuscripts read the pronoun "you" ("for you are like ten thousand of us").
notes.18:8: Qere reads the Niphal feminine singular participle "spread out," agreeing with singular "battle," whereas Ketiv has a feminine plural form.
notes.18:12: Qere reads the conditional particle "even if" for Ketiv's variant spelling. In the embedded quote, MT has the indefinite pronoun mi ("whoever you are") after "protect," whereas several ancient versions read li ("for me").
notes.18:13: Qere reads "against my own life," whereas Ketiv reads "against his life" (referring to Absalom).
notes.18:22: Literally "and for you there is no news/reward finding [you]"; the Hebrew noun besorah can mean either "news" or "reward for bringing news" (cf. 2 Sam 4:10), with the Qal participle indicating a reward coming to him.
notes.18:29: The Hebrew syntax places the subject "Joab" between the two direct objects "the king's servant" (the Cushite) and "your servant" (Ahimaaz); some instead construe "the king's servant Joab" as the subject sending Ahimaaz.
notes.19:7: For "if," the qere reads lu ("if"), introducing the counterfactual condition, while the ketiv is spelled lo ("not," possibly an orthographic variant of lu).
notes.19:32: For "across the Jordan" at the end of the verse, the qere reads et-hayyarden ("across the Jordan"), while the ketiv reads bayyarden ("at the Jordan").
notes.19:41: For "had brought [the king] across," the qere reads the Hiphil perfect he'eviru following the fronted subject, while the ketiv reads a prefixed form with waw (wy'brw).
notes.19:43: "Has any gift been given to us" translates nisse't nissa' lanu, combining nisse't (either a noun meaning "gift/portion" or an unusual Niphal infinitive absolute) with nissa' (Niphal perfect of nasa').
notes.19:44: "In David as well we have more than you" translates the terse Masoretic Hebrew wegam-bedawid ani mimmekha ("and also in David I [have more] than you"), where the men of Israel speak collectively in the first-person singular.
notes.20:3: "In living widowhood" translates almenut chayyut (literally "widowhood of life"), describing their status as living widows while David remained alive.
notes.20:5: For "he delayed," the qere reads wayyocher (from the root achar/yachar), while the ketiv is spelled wyyhr.
notes.20:6: "Escape from our sight" translates wehitzil enenu (Hiphil of natzal plus "our eye/eyes"), literally "deliver [himself from] our eye(s)" or "snatch away our eye(s)," understood idiomatically as slipping out of reach.
notes.20:14: For "they assembled," the qere reads wayyiqqahalu (Niphal of qahal), correcting the transposed letters of the ketiv (wyqlhw); "the Berites" (habberim) renders the Masoretic gentilic directly.
notes.20:23: For "the Cherethites," the qere reads hakkereti (matching 20:7), while the ketiv reads hakkari ("the Carites").
notes.20:25: For the name "Sheva," the qere reads Sheva, while the ketiv is spelled Sheya.
notes.21:6: "Impale" translates the Hiphil of yaqa' (also in v. 9; Hophal participle in v. 13), a rare verb whose exact mode of public execution or exposure is uncertain. The Qere reads the Hophal yuttan ("let ... be given"), whereas the Ketiv has the Niphal form yntn.
notes.21:8: The Masoretic Text reads "Michal" and "she had borne," whereas 1 Sam 18:19 identifies Merab as the wife of Adriel the Meholathite and 2 Sam 6:23 states that Michal had no child.
notes.21:16: Ishbi-benob follows the Qere (weyishbi; Ketiv wyshbw), and "Rapha" (also in vv. 18, 20, 22) renders Hebrew ha-raphah, with the definite article, designating an eponymous giant figure linked with the Rephaim. Hebrew literally says "girded with a new [feminine]," with "sword" implied by the feminine adjective hadashah.
notes.21:19: The Masoretic Text attributes the killing of Goliath the Gittite here to Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim (lit. "Jaare of weavers," echoing "weavers' beam" at the end of the verse); the parallel in 1 Chr 20:5 has Elhanan son of Jair striking down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite.
notes.21:20: The Qere reads madon ("stature," from the root mdd; cf. 1 Chr 20:6), whereas the Ketiv reads mdyn (a plural form of mad, "measure").
notes.22:33: The form wayyatter is pointed as a Hiphil wayyiqtol of ntr ('loosen, set free, clear'), rendered here as 'clears' (some lexicographers instead connect it to twr, 'guide, direct'). The qere reads darki ('my way'), followed here, whereas the ketiv reads darko ('his way').
notes.22:34: The qere reads raglay ('my feet'), followed here in harmony with the first-person suffixes in verses 33-34, whereas the ketiv reads raglaw ('his feet').
notes.22:36: The form anotekha is morphologically the Qal infinitive construct of anah ('answer, respond') with a second-person masculine singular suffix ('Your answering'); compare Psalm 18:36, which reads the noun anwatekha ('Your humility' or 'Your gentleness').
notes.22:46: The verb weyahgeru (Qal of hgr, 'limp, hobble' in comparative Semitic usage, with the pregnant preposition 'out of') is rendered 'come limping out of'; compare Psalm 18:46, which reads the metathesized weyahregu ('come trembling out of').
notes.22:51: The qere reads the noun migdol ('tower of'), followed here in a construct chain ('the tower of His king's salvation'), whereas the ketiv reads the Hiphil participle magdil ('making great' or 'magnifying').
notes.23:5: Both clauses introduced by ki lo function as rhetorical negative questions without an explicit interrogative particle. The final verb is Hiphil (cause to sprout), echoing the sprouting grass of verse 4.
notes.23:8: The Masoretic Text reads 'he was Adino the Eznite' with Qere ha-etsni (Ketiv ha-etsno) and Qere feminine echat (Ketiv masculine echad) to agree with feminine pa'am; the parallel in 1 Chronicles 11:11 instead reads 'he wielded his spear.'
notes.23:13: Qere reads sheloshah ('three'), while Ketiv reads sheloshim ('thirty'). The Masoretic Text also reads 'at harvest time' (el-qatsir), where 1 Chronicles 11:15 has 'to the rock' (al-hatsur).
notes.23:18: Qere reads ha-sheloshah ('the three'), while Ketiv reads ha-sheloshi ('the captains' or a defective spelling of 'the thirty'). The Masoretic Text likewise reads 'the three' twice in verse 19 (compare 'the thirty' in verse 23).
notes.23:20: Qere reads chayil ('valor', Ketiv chay) and ha-ari ('lion', Ketiv ha-aryeh). The term ariel ('Ariels of Moab') is uncertain and is often understood as a title for lion-like champions.
notes.24:5: Hebrew yemin literally means 'right side,' which denotes south when facing east. The phrase 'the valley of Gad' renders the unusual double-definite construction ha-nachal ha-Gad in the Masoretic Text.
notes.24:13: The Masoretic Text reads 'seven years of famine,' whereas the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 21:12 reads 'three years.'
notes.24:16: Qere reads ha-Arawnah ('Araunah,' with the definite article), while Ketiv reads ha-Awarnah; similarly in verse 18 Qere reads Arawnah for Ketiv Aranyah.
notes.24:23: Following the Masoretic accentuation, ha-melekh stands in apposition to Araunah ('Araunah the king gave to the king'); many interpreters instead read ha-melekh as a vocative continuing Araunah's speech from verse 22 ('All of this, King, Araunah gives to the king').
